newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark says EU referendum not before March 1998.
newsitem.headline: Denmark says EU referendum not before March 1998.

text.p: Denmark will hold a referendum on last June's Amsterdam amendments to the European Union treaty some time after mid-March 1998, Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said on Tuesday.

"That gives us plenty of time for debate. We have only just begun the discussion and the referendum will be in seven months from now, at the earliest," he told reporters at the ministry's weekly briefing.
He said the government would propose a firm date after parliament reconvenes in October from its summer recess, and there would then be further debate.

Opponents of EU membership say they expect the Supreme Court to rule in March on a suit they have entered challenging the legality of Danish EU membership. But Petersen said he expected a verdict earlier.
The petitioners say Denmark has ceded authority to supranational institutions such as the European Court to an extent that breaches its own constitution.
Danes are traditionally cool toward the EU and shocked their fellow members in 1992 by flatly rejecting the Maastricht Treaty on closer European cooperation in a referendum.
They only voted to ratify the treaty the following year on condition that Denmark opt out of economic and monetary union, a joint defence structure, cross-border policing and a common asylum policy.
In an opinion poll last week, 32 percent of respondents said they would vote to accept the Amsterdam treaty, 31 percent would reject it and 36.5 percent were unsure.

EU leaders decided at Amsterdam to leave the Western European Union defence grouping independent of the EU, to grant Britain and Ireland opt-outs from a plan to lift internal border checks, to make job creation a formal EU goal, and to increase cooperation in foreign policy and asylum policy.
The summit left key institutional reforms to be taken early next century.

Petersen and Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen have warned that a referendum "no" vote would not only prevent the Amsterdam amendments going into force but also undermine Denmark's efforts to expand the EU eastward.
And they say Danish hesitancy on the EU would inevitably lessen its influence in the bloc.

Politicians in both the opposition and ruling centre-left coalition have labelled such comments as scaremongering and say that attempts to scare voters into a "yes" vote could panic them instead into rejecting the treaty.
